name: Bromantane

lead: Bromantane is a Russian-developed adamantane drug, sold there as Ladasten for neurasthenia. People use it for motivation, calmer social stress and a steadier training drive, and some claim it also lifts testosterone for physique gains.

Animal research reports it increases the enzymes that make dopamine rather than mainly blocking its reuptake. Most human evidence is from Russian-language studies; the testosterone and physique claims circulate in forums and have not been tested in published human trials.

paras: Used as an oral nootropic, typically for motivation and stress resilience during demanding training or work periods. It is often discussed alongside recovery routines.

Russian studies report few side effects (about 3% of patients in one large study), but long-term data in healthy users are lacking. It is prescription-only in Russia, not FDA-approved, and banned by WADA since 1997, which matters for tested athletes.

angle.text: Bromantane is taken for motivation and lower social stress, with users linking that to better training drive and physique results, and some claim it raises testosterone. Human data are small and mostly Russian-language, and the physique claims are anecdotal.

lead: Bromantane (also spelled bromantan; Russian brand name Ladasten) is a synthetic adamantane derivative, chemically N-(4-bromophenyl)adamantan-2-amine, that is related to amantadine and memantine. It is described in the literature as an atypical stimulant and anxiolytic and as an "actoprotector", a term used in Russian pharmacology for synthetic adaptogens said to raise resistance to physical and psychological stress. [1][2][3]

Bromantane was developed in the Soviet Union at the Zakusov Institute of Pharmacology in Moscow and is a prescription drug in Russia for neurasthenia (asthenia). It is not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, and it has been on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list since 1997. [2] In looksmaxxing and nootropic circles it is discussed as a supplement for motivation, mood, stress resilience and recovery rather than as a direct appearance treatment. [4][5]

Most published human data are from Russian-language journals. Animal studies report that it increases the activity of enzymes involved in dopamine synthesis. [2][6][7] Proponents' claims about testosterone, prolactin and sexual function that circulate in forums have not been tested in published human trials.
infobox: Reported 42% oral bioavailability; about 11 hours in humans [2]
Rx-only in Russia; unscheduled and not FDA-approved in the US; banned in sport (WADA) [2]

paras: In Russia bromantane is approved for neurasthenia, a fatigue-and-weakness syndrome, and it is described as combining mild stimulant and anxiolytic effects. [2] Russian military and sports medicine reportedly used it to shorten recovery after heavy physical exertion. [2]

Outside Russia it is sold or traded as a nootropic or research chemical. Forum users describe taking it for motivation, drive, calmer mood and as a complement to training and stress management. [4][5]

Unlike amphetamine-type stimulants, bromantane is reported to act mainly by raising the expression of tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, enzymes in dopamine synthesis, rather than primarily blocking the dopamine transporter. [2] A 1995 rat study reported changes in dopamine, serotonin and their metabolites in several brain regions after acute and chronic administration, and a microdialysis study in the same year examined dopamine release in the striatum. [6][7]

Researchers also describe effects on protein kinase signalling and neurotrophin expression in animals, but the receptor responsible has not been identified and the full mechanism remains unclear. [2] Reviews of Russian adaptogen research list bromantane among synthetic actoprotectors. [3][8]

Reported oral bioavailability is about 42%, with onset in roughly 1.5 to 2 hours, a duration of 8 to 12 hours and an elimination half-life near 11 hours in humans. The main metabolite is 6-beta-hydroxybromantane. [2]

The best-cited human evidence is a multicentre Russian study of 728 patients with asthenia that reported symptom improvement on clinical global scales, with persistence after treatment ended. [2] A 2009 placebo comparison in neurasthenia is also cited. [2] Most of this literature is in Russian-language journals, and independent replication in Western trials has not been published. [2][9]
No controlled study has examined bromantane for appearance outcomes, body composition, hormone levels in healthy people, or the stress-and-recovery effects claimed in forums.

Russian sources describe the drug as well tolerated. In the multicentre study, side effects were reported in about 3% of patients, none serious, and 0.8% stopped treatment because of them. [2] Absence of dependence and withdrawal is reported mainly in Russian-language and animal work. [2][9]

Animal toxicity studies at very high doses have reported neurological effects, which some authors attribute to anticholinergic activity. [2] Long-term safety in healthy adults using it recreationally has not been studied in published trials.

Amantadine was developed as an influenza antiviral in the 1960s, and its dopaminergic effects were noticed in 1969. Bromantane emerged in the 1980s from Soviet work on adamantane derivatives intended to increase resistance to extreme conditions; a Russian review describes 329 novel adamantane derivatives synthesised and studied, of which bromantane was among the most promising. [2][9]

At the 1996 Atlanta Olympics several Russian athletes tested positive, bringing the drug to international attention, and WADA listed it as a stimulant and masking agent in 1997. [2][1] It was repurposed in Russia as a neurasthenia treatment, with the Ladasten brand approved in the late 2000s. [2]
Bromantane is prescription-only in Russia, banned in sport by WADA, and unscheduled but not approved by the FDA in the United States. [2]

Forum threads on looksmax.org present bromantane as a dopamine-supporting compound that increases motivation, lowers anxiety, and may help users on stimulant medication, citing Wikipedia and Russian literature. [4][5] Users trade impressions of effect from oral and other routes; some report little effect. [4]

Published human data consist mainly of Russian-language studies in asthenia and neurasthenia, including a 728-patient multicentre study, and military and sports-medicine reports. [2][9] No studies found in healthy people for appearance, hormonal or looksmaxxing-related outcomes.

lore.intro: Bromantane is discussed on looksmax.org as a dopamine-boosting nootropic for drive and stress, often alongside other recovery and mood compounds. [4][5]

It lowers anxiety and social stress
It boosts testosterone and lowers prolactin, aiding physique
It resensitises users to stimulants such as caffeine or methylphenidate
It is non-addictive and has minimal side effects
